## 11.5 Summary & 8-Problem 4-Tier Practice Ladder

Let us now synthesize every tool from Sections 11.1–11.4 across our canonical 8-problem practice ladder. Every problem below is completely self-contained with progressive hints and a full derivation from first principles.

---

### Stepping Stone 1 (`#003`) — Colored Paper / Colored Tree (Implicit Parity & 2-Colored Tree EGF)

- **Source**: [AtCoder `fps_24_f` — Colored Paper](https://atcoder.jp/contests/fps-24/tasks/fps_24_f) (Curriculum Pool `#003`, `1A#2` & `3B#1`)
- **Prerequisites**: Chapter 4 (Labeled `SET` construction & Prüfer sequences), §11.2 (LIF Form 1 & Form 2)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

Count the number of rooted labeled trees on $N$ vertices ($1 \le N \le 2.5 \times 10^5$) in which **every vertex has an even number of children** ($0, 2, 4, \dots$), modulo $998244353$. *(In the complete solution below, we also treat the closely related 2-colored red-blue unrooted and alternating rooted tree EGF variants on $N$ vertices partitioned into $R$ red and $B = N - R$ blue vertices.)*

**Required Complexity**: $O(N \log N)$ time and $O(N)$ space.

**Sample Trace ($N \le 4$):** For $N = 1, 2, 3, 4$, the counts of rooted labeled trees where every vertex has an even number of children are $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = 0$, $a_3 = 3$ (any of the $3$ vertices can serve as the root with the remaining $2$ vertices as its children), and $a_4 = 0$ (since $N - 1$ equals the sum of even out-degrees, $N$ must be odd for a valid tree to exist).

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model</summary>

In Part A, a rooted labeled tree consists of a labeled root $x$ together with an unordered set of subtrees whose size is forced to be **even**. What is the labeled `SET` operator restricted to even sizes? In Part B, recall from Prüfer sequences that vertex $i$ has degree $d_i$ in an unrooted labeled tree if and only if $i$ appears $d_i - 1$ times in the Prüfer sequence of length $N - 2$.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad</summary>

For Part A, the even-size `SET` operator is $\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{u^{2k}}{(2k)!} = \cosh(u) = \frac{e^u + e^{-u}}{2}$, so the EGF $F(x)$ satisfies $F(x) = x \cosh(F(x))$. This is in standard LIF Form 1 with $\phi(u) = \cosh(u)$! For the coupled rooted system $R(x) = x e^{B(x)}, B(x) = x P(R(x))$, substitute $B(x)$ into $R(x)$ to get $R(x) = x \exp\bigl(x P(R(x))\bigr)$ and look at the bundled variable $W(x) = x P(R(x))$ or rescale $R(x)/x$.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract</summary>

Apply LIF Form 1 to $F(x) = x \cosh(F(x))$: $[x^N] F(x) = \frac{1}{N} [u^{N-1}] \cosh(u)^N$. Expand $\cosh(u)^N = 2^{-N} (e^u + e^{-u})^N = 2^{-N} \sum_{j=0}^N \binom{N}{j} e^{(2j-N)u}$ using the binomial theorem to extract $[u^{N-1}]$ in $O(N \log N)$ (or $O(N)$) time!

</details>

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation & Solution"}

#### Part A: Rooted Labeled Trees with Even Out-Degree ($F(x) = x \cosh(F(x))$)

1. **Combinatorial Specification to EGF**: Let $F(x) = \sum_{N=1}^\infty a_N \frac{x^N}{N!}$ be the exponential generating function of rooted labeled trees where every vertex has an even number of children. A vertex has $2k$ children ($k \ge 0$) by choosing an unordered set of $2k$ rooted subtrees, represented by $\frac{F(x)^{2k}}{(2k)!}$. Summing over all $k \ge 0$ and multiplying by $x$ for the root label gives
   $$
   F(x) = x \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{F(x)^{2k}}{(2k)!} = x \cosh(F(x)), \quad \text{where } \phi(u) = \cosh(u) = \frac{e^u + e^{-u}}{2}.
   $$
2. **Lagrange Inversion (Form 1)**: Since $\phi(0) = \cosh(0) = 1 \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times$ and $N < 998244353$, Form 1 of Lagrange Inversion gives
   $$
   [x^N] F(x) = \frac{1}{N} [u^{N-1}] \bigl(\cosh u\bigr)^N = \frac{1}{N \cdot 2^N} [u^{N-1}] \bigl(e^u + e^{-u}\bigr)^N.
   $$
3. **Binomial Expansion & Coefficient Extraction**: Notice that $\cosh(u)$ is an **even** function ($\cosh(-u) = \cosh(u)$), so $\cosh(u)^N$ contains only even powers of $u$. Thus if $N - 1$ is odd (i.e., **$N$ is even**), $[u^{N-1}]\cosh(u)^N = 0$ immediately! (Combinatorially, in any tree with even out-degrees, the total number of non-root vertices $\sum c(v_i)$ is even, so $N = 1 + \sum c(v_i)$ must be odd.)
   When **$N$ is odd**, expand $(e^u + e^{-u})^N$ via the binomial theorem:
   $$
   (e^u + e^{-u})^N = \sum_{j=0}^N \binom{N}{j} e^{j u} e^{-(N-j)u} = \sum_{j=0}^N \binom{N}{j} e^{(2j - N)u}.
   $$
   Extracting $[u^{N-1}] e^{(2j-N)u} = \frac{(2j - N)^{N-1}}{(N - 1)!}$ and multiplying by $N!$ to recover $a_N = N! [x^N] F(x)$ yields the closed-form sum
   $$
   a_N = N! \cdot \frac{1}{N \cdot 2^N} \sum_{j=0}^N \binom{N}{j} \frac{(2j - N)^{N-1}}{(N - 1)!} = \frac{1}{2^N} \sum_{j=0}^N \binom{N}{j} (2j - N)^{N - 1} \pmod{998244353}.
   $$
   This evaluates in $O(N \log N)$ time (or $O(N)$ using a linear sieve for $(2j-N)^{N-1}$) and $O(N)$ space.

#### Part B: 2-Colored Red-Blue Parity Unrooted Trees & Coupled Rooted Trees

1. **Unrooted Degree-Parity Variant**: By the Prüfer bijection, unrooted trees on $N$ labeled vertices with degrees $d_1, \dots, d_N$ correspond to sequences of length $N - 2$ where vertex $i$ appears $d_i - 1$ times.
   - If vertex $i$ is **red** ($d_i$ odd), then $d_i - 1$ is **even**, so its EGF factor in the sequence is $\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{u^{2k}}{(2k)!} = \cosh(u)$.
   - If vertex $i$ is **blue** ($d_i$ even), then $d_i - 1 \ge 1$ is **odd**, so its EGF factor is $\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{u^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!} = \sinh(u)$.
   Therefore, with $R$ red and $B = N - R$ blue vertices, the count is
   $$
   \text{Ans} = (N - 2)! [u^{N-2}] \Bigl( \cosh(u)^R \sinh(u)^{N - R} \Bigr) = \frac{(N-2)!}{2^N} [u^{N-2}] \Bigl( (e^u + e^{-u})^R (e^u - e^{-u})^{N - R} \Bigr).
   $$
   Expanding the product $(1 + z)^R (1 - z)^{N - R} = \sum_{j=0}^N c_j z^j$ in $O(N \log N)$ time gives $\text{Ans} = 2^{-N} \sum_{j=0}^N c_j (2j - N)^{N - 2}$.
2. **Coupled Rooted Variant ($R(x) = x e^{B(x)}, B(x) = x P(R(x))$ where $P(u) = \sum_{j=0}^K \frac{u^j}{j!}$)**: Substituting $B(x) = x P(R(x))$ into $R(x) = x e^{B(x)}$ gives $R(x) = x \exp\bigl(x P(R(x))\bigr)$. Notice that $\frac{R(x)}{x} = \exp\bigl(x P(R(x))\bigr)$, so $[x^N] R(x) = [x^{N-1}] \exp\bigl(x P(R(x))\bigr)$ can be extracted by bipartite LIF (see `Adv-1` `#010` below): for a fixed $(N_R, N_B)$ of red and blue vertices ($N_R + N_B = N$),
   $$
   [x_R^{N_R} x_B^{N_B}] R = [u_R^{N_R} u_B^{N_B}] \, u_R \left(1 - \frac{u_R u_B P'(u_R)}{P(u_R)}\right) e^{N_R u_B} P(u_R)^{N_B},
   $$
   which decouples into $[u_B^{N_B}] e^{N_R u_B} = \frac{N_R^{N_B}}{N_B!}$ and a single 1D polynomial power $P(u_R)^{N_B}$ in $O(N \log N)$ time!

::: {.callout-important}
## Algorithm Contract (`#003` AtCoder `fps_24_f` — Colored Paper)

- **Input**: Integer $N \le 2.5 \times 10^5$ (and optional red vertex count $R \le N$ for Part B), prime $p = 998244353$.
- **Output**: Number of valid labeled trees $a_N \bmod 998244353$.
- **Index & Truncation Boundaries**: For Part A, return $0$ immediately if $N \equiv 0 \pmod 2$; for odd $N$, sum $j \in [0, N]$ using precomputed factorials up to $N$. For Part B, expand $(1+z)^R(1-z)^{N-R}$ up to degree $N$.
- **1-Sentence Loop Invariant**: After processing index $j \in [0, r]$, the accumulator holds $2^{-N} \sum_{i=0}^r \binom{N}{i} (2i - N)^{N-1} \bmod p$, which equals $[u^{N-1}] \text{ of the first } r+1 \text{ binomial terms of } \cosh(u)^N$.
- **Complexity**: $O(N \log N)$ time (or $O(N)$ with linear sieve) and $O(N)$ space.
:::

### Stepping Stone 2 (`#200`) — [AGM 2021] 恐龙 / [KrOI2021] Maple Leaf Story

- **Source**: [Luogu P7438 — [AGM 2021] 恐龙 / Maple Leaf Story](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P7438) (Curriculum Pool `#200`, `3B#28` & `3A#7`)
- **Prerequisites**: Chapter 3 (`ln`, `exp`, `pow`), §11.2 (LIF Form 1 & Form 2)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

Let $F(x) \in \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]$ ($p = 998244353$) be the formal power series with $[x^0] F(x) = 0$ defined implicitly by
$$
F(x) = x \phi(F(x)),
$$
where $\phi(u) = \sum_{i=0}^d \phi_i u^i$ is a given polynomial with $\phi_0 = \phi(0) \neq 0$ (in the canonical special case of *Maple Leaf Story*, $\phi(u) = 1 + u + \frac{u^2}{2}$, corresponding to unary-binary labeled trees / Motzkin trees). Given $N \le 2 \times 10^5$ (and a power exponent $1 \le k \le N$), compute modulo $998244353$ the composite ordered-forest extraction
$$
[x^N] \frac{1}{1 - F(x)} = \sum_{k=1}^N [x^N] F(x)^k
$$
(the total number of ordered forests of $F$-trees of total size $N$, obtained by upgrading the single-power coefficient extraction $[x^N] F(x)^k$ via Composite Lagrange Inversion).

**Required Complexity**: $O(N \log N)$ time for general $\phi(u)$ (and $O(N)$ time when $\phi(u) = 1 + u + \frac{u^2}{2}$ is sparse of degree $2$).

**Sample Trace ($N \le 4$):** For $\phi(u) = 1 + u + \frac{u^2}{2}$, iterating $F(x) = x\bigl(1 + F(x) + \frac{1}{2}F(x)^2\bigr)$ yields $F(x) = x + x^2 + \frac{3}{2}x^3 + \frac{8}{3}x^4 + O(x^5)$. Thus for $N = 3, k = 1$, Task 1 gives $[x^3]F(x) = \frac{3}{2} \equiv 499122178 \pmod{998244353}$, and Task 2 gives $[x^3]\frac{1}{1-F(x)} = [x^3]\bigl(F + F^2 + F^3\bigr) = \frac{3}{2} + 2 + 1 = \frac{9}{2} \equiv 499122181 \pmod{998244353}$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model</summary>

In Task 1, we want $[x^N] F(x)^k$ for a single fixed pair $(N, k)$ where $F(x) = x \phi(F(x))$. In Task 2, we want $[x^N] H(F(x))$ where $H(u) = \frac{1}{1 - u}$ is a rational function of $F(x)$. Which two forms of Lagrange Inversion apply directly without ever solving for $F(x)$ via Newton's method?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad</summary>

For Task 1, apply **Form 1** ($[x^N] F(x)^k = \frac{k}{N} [u^{N-k}] \phi(u)^N$). For Task 2, compare Form 1 ($H'(u) = \frac{1}{(1-u)^2}$) with **Form 2 (`另类拉格朗日反演`)**:
$$
[x^N] \frac{1}{1 - F(x)} = [u^N] \left( \frac{\phi(u) - u\phi'(u)}{1 - u} \phi(u)^{N-1} \right).
$$
Notice that for $\phi(u) = 1 + u + \frac{u^2}{2}$, $\phi(u) - u\phi'(u) = 1 - \frac{u^2}{2}$!

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract</summary>

To evaluate $[u^{N-k}] \phi(u)^N$ or $[u^N] \frac{\phi(u) - u\phi'(u)}{1 - u} \phi(u)^{N-1}$ for general $\phi(u)$, compute $\phi(u)^N \bmod u^{N+1}$ in $O(N \log N)$ time using a single polynomial `ln` and `exp`. When $\phi(u) = 1 + u + \frac{u^2}{2}$, $P(u) = \phi(u)^{N-1}$ satisfies the 3-term ODE $\phi(u) P'(u) = (N-1)\phi'(u)P(u)$, allowing all coefficients of $P(u)$ up to $u^N$ to be computed in $O(N)$ time!

</details>

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation & Solution"}

#### 1. Task 1: Extracting $[x^N] F(x)^k$ via Form 1

Since $F(x) = x\phi(F(x))$ with $\phi(0) \neq 0$ and $1 \le N < 998244353$, Form 1 of Lagrange–Bürmann Inversion with $H(u) = u^k$ gives:
$$
[x^N] F(x)^k = \frac{k}{N} [u^{N - k}] \phi(u)^N.
$$

- If $k > N$ (or $k = 0 < N$), the coefficient is $0$ (and for $N = k = 0$, $[x^0]F(x)^0 = 1$).
- For $1 \le k \le N$, we truncate $\phi(u)$ modulo $u^{N - k + 1}$ and compute $\phi(u)^N = \phi_0^N \exp\bigl(N \ln(\phi_0^{-1}\phi(u))\bigr) \bmod u^{N - k + 1}$ in **$O((N-k)\log(N-k))$** time.

#### 2. Task 2: Extracting $[x^N] \frac{1}{1 - F(x)}$ via Form 2 (`另类拉格朗日反演`)

Let $H(u) = \frac{1}{1 - u}$. By Form 2 of Lagrange Inversion (valid even at $N = 0$),
$$
[x^N] \frac{1}{1 - F(x)} = [u^N] \left( \frac{1}{1 - u} \left(1 - \frac{u\phi'(u)}{\phi(u)}\right) \phi(u)^N \right) = [u^N] \left( \frac{\phi(u) - u\phi'(u)}{1 - u} \cdot \phi(u)^{N - 1} \right).
$$
Let $P(u) := \phi(u)^{N-1} = \sum_{j=0}^N p_j u^j \bmod u^{N+1}$ and $Q(u) := \phi(u) - u\phi'(u) = \sum_{i=0}^d (1 - i)\phi_i u^i$. Since multiplying by $\frac{1}{1 - u} = \sum_{m=0}^\infty u^m$ simply takes the prefix sum of coefficients, we don't even need a full polynomial multiplication at the end:
$$
[x^N] \frac{1}{1 - F(x)} = \sum_{m=0}^N [u^m] \bigl( Q(u) P(u) \bigr).
$$

#### 3. $O(N)$ Linear-Time Specialization for $\phi(u) = 1 + u + \frac{u^2}{2}$

When $\phi(u) = 1 + u + \frac{u^2}{2}$, we have $\phi'(u) = 1 + u$, so $Q(u) = \phi(u) - u\phi'(u) = \left(1 + u + \frac{u^2}{2}\right) - (u + u^2) = 1 - \frac{u^2}{2}$. Furthermore, $P(u) = \phi(u)^{N-1}$ satisfies
$$
\left(1 + u + \frac{u^2}{2}\right) P'(u) = (N - 1)(1 + u) P(u).
$$
Extracting $[u^j]$ on both sides gives the 3-term linear recurrence for $p_j = [u^j] \phi(u)^{N-1}$:
$$
(j + 1) p_{j+1} = (N - 1 - j) p_j + \left(N - 1 - \frac{j - 1}{2}\right) p_{j-1} \quad (j \ge 0, \; p_0 = 1, \; p_{-1} = 0).
$$
Computing $p_0, \dots, p_N$ via this 3-term recurrence and summing $[u^m]\bigl((1 - u^2/2)P(u)\bigr)$ solves the problem in **$O(N)$ time** using linear modular inverses!

::: {.callout-note}
## Dual-Perspective Cross-Reference: Single-$N$ LIF vs. All-$n$ Kinoshita–Li Composition (`Ch 21.3`)

In Problem `#200`, we needed $[x^N] H(F(x))$ for a **single** target degree $N$, which Lagrange Inversion reduced to a single polynomial power $\phi(u)^N$ in $O(N \log N)$ time. What if a problem instead asks for $[x^n] F(x)$ across **all** $n = 1, 2, \dots, N$ for a high-degree polynomial $\phi(u)$? Running LIF separately for each $n$ would take $O(N^2 \log N)$ time, whereas computing the compositional inverse of $G(u) = \frac{u}{\phi(u)}$ for all degrees $1 \dots N$ simultaneously takes **$O(N \log^2 N)$** time via the **Kinoshita–Li power projection / compositional inverse algorithm** developed in **Chapter 21 (`Ch 21.3`)**. Always match the engine to the query regime: **single $N \implies$ LIF in $O(N \log N)$**; **all $n \le N$ for high-degree $\phi \implies$ Newton (`Ch 10`) or Kinoshita–Li (`Ch 21.3`)**.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Algorithm Contract (`#200` Luogu P7438 — Maple Leaf Story)

- **Input**: Polynomial $\phi(u)$ with $\phi(0) \neq 0$, target degree $N \le 2 \times 10^5$, and power $k \le N$.
- **Output**: $[x^N] F(x)^k \bmod p$ (Task 1) and $[x^N] \frac{1}{1-F(x)} \bmod p$ (Task 2).
- **Index & Truncation Boundaries**: Truncate $\phi(u)$ modulo $u^{N-k+1}$ for Task 1 and modulo $u^{N+1}$ for Task 2. For the 3-term ODE recurrence on $P(u) = (1 + u + u^2/2)^{N-1}$, initialize $p_0 = 1, p_{-1} = 0$ and iterate $j = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1$.
- **1-Sentence Loop Invariant**: After step $j$ of the ODE recurrence, $p_0, \dots, p_{j+1}$ equal the exact coefficients $[u^0], \dots, [u^{j+1}]$ of $\phi(u)^{N-1} \bmod p$.
- **Complexity**: $O(N \log N)$ time for general $\phi(u)$ ($O(N)$ time for $\phi(u) = 1 + u + u^2/2$) and $O(N)$ space.
:::

### Intermediate 1 (`#196`) — [清华集训2016] 你的生命已如风中残烛 (Raney's Cycle Lemma on Card-Draw Permutations)

- **Source**: [Luogu P6672 — [清华集训2016] 你的生命已如风中残烛](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P6672) (Curriculum Pool `#196`, `4B#5`)
- **Prerequisites**: §11.3.4 (Raney's Cycle Lemma, Theorem 11.2)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

You have a deck of $m$ distinct cards. Among them, $n$ are **special cards** with positive integer draw weights $w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n \ge 1$ satisfying
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n w_i = m,
$$
and the remaining $m - n$ cards are **normal cards** with draw weight $w_i = 0$ ($n < i \le m$).

You start with $1$ card in your hand (or equivalently, you arrange all $m$ cards in a permutation $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_m$ and begin with $1$ action point; playing card $p_j$ costs $1$ action point and grants $w_{p_j}$ new action points, changing your net action points by $w_{p_j} - 1$). A permutation $(p_1, \dots, p_m)$ of the $m$ cards is **valid** if your action points remain strictly positive ($\ge 1$) after each of the first $m - 1$ cards, so that you successfully play all $m$ cards (ending with $1 + \sum_{j=1}^m (w_{p_j} - 1) = 1 + 0 = 1$ action point after the $m$-th card, or $0$ after playing one final dummy $0$-weight card).

Given $n \le 40$ and $w_1, \dots, w_n$ with $m = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i \le 10^5$, compute the number of valid permutations of the $m$ cards modulo $998244353$.

**Required Complexity**: $O(m)$ time and $O(1)$ space!

**Sample Trace ($N \le 4$):** Suppose $n = 1$ and $w_1 = 3$, so $m = 3$ with $1$ special card of weight $3$ and $m - n = 2$ normal cards of weight $0$. For distinct normal cards $0_A, 0_B$, only the $2$ permutations $(3, 0_A, 0_B)$ and $(3, 0_B, 0_A)$ keep action points strictly positive ($1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 1$), giving $\frac{m!}{m - n + 1} = \frac{6}{3} = 2$ (and $\frac{m!}{(m - n + 1)!} = \frac{6}{6} = 1$ when normal cards are indistinguishable).

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model</summary>

Look at the net change $a_j := w_{p_j} - 1$ at step $j$: since $w_i \ge 0$, every step satisfies **$a_j \ge -1$**, and the only steps with $a_j = -1$ are the $m - n$ normal cards (weight $0$). Furthermore, the sum over all $m$ cards is $\sum_{i=1}^m (w_i - 1) = m - m = 0$, while the condition is $1 + \sum_{j=1}^r a_j \ge 1 \iff \sum_{j=1}^r a_j \ge 0$ for all $1 \le r \le m$. What cyclic-shift invariant governs integer sequences bounded below by $-1$ whose prefix sums stay nonnegative?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad</summary>

This is the exact signature of **Raney's Cycle Lemma (Theorem 11.2)**! Raney's Lemma requires the total sum of the sequence to be $-1$ (not $0$). How do we turn a sequence of $m$ steps with sum $0$ and all prefix sums $\ge 0$ into a sequence of $m + 1$ steps with sum $-1$ and all proper prefix sums $\ge 0$? Append a **single dummy normal card** $w_{m+1} = 0$ ($a_{m+1} = -1$) at the very end of the permutation!

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract</summary>

Now consider all $(m + 1)!$ permutations of the $m + 1$ cards (which consist of the $n$ special cards and $m - n + 1$ normal cards of weight $0$). Group every $(m+1)!$ permutation into cyclic orbits of size $m + 1$. By Raney's Lemma, how many shifts in each orbit of size $m + 1$ are valid? And why must the last card of any valid sequence of length $m + 1$ automatically be one of the $m - n + 1$ normal cards?

</details>

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation & Solution"}

#### 1. Translating the Card Process to Raney's Cycle Lemma

For each card $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, define its net step value $a_i := w_i - 1$.

- For the $n$ special cards ($1 \le i \le n$), $w_i \ge 1 \implies a_i \ge 0$.
- For the $m - n$ normal cards ($n + 1 \le i \le m$), $w_i = 0 \implies a_i = -1$.
- The total sum of all $m$ step values is
  $$
  \sum_{i=1}^m a_i = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i - m = m - m = 0.
  $$
A permutation $(p_1, \dots, p_m)$ of $\{1, \dots, m\}$ is valid if and only if all prefix sums are nonnegative:
$$
\sum_{j=1}^r a_{p_j} \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } 1 \le r \le m.
$$

#### 2. Appending the $(m+1)$-st Dummy Card to Create Sum $-1$

Introduce one additional normal card with label $m + 1$ and weight $w_{m+1} = 0$, so $a_{m+1} = -1$. Now we have $m + 1$ distinct cards in total:

- $n$ special cards with $a_i \ge 0$, and
- $(m - n + 1)$ normal cards with $a_i = -1$,

whose total sum is
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{m+1} a_i = 0 + (-1) = -1.
$$
Suppose $(\pi_1, \pi_2, \dots, \pi_{m+1})$ is any permutation of $\{1, 2, \dots, m + 1\}$ that is **$1$-valid in the sense of Raney's Lemma (Theorem 11.2)**—meaning that
$$
\sum_{j=1}^r a_{\pi_j} \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } 1 \le r \le m, \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{j=1}^{m+1} a_{\pi_j} = -1.
$$
Look at the last step $\pi_{m+1}$ of any such $1$-valid permutation: since $\sum_{j=1}^m a_{\pi_j} \ge 0$ and $\sum_{j=1}^{m+1} a_{\pi_j} = -1$, we have
$$
a_{\pi_{m+1}} = -1 - \sum_{j=1}^m a_{\pi_j} \le -1.
$$
Because $a_i \ge -1$ for all cards, this forces **$a_{\pi_{m+1}} = -1$** and $\sum_{j=1}^m a_{\pi_j} = 0$! That means:

1. In *every* $1$-valid permutation $(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_{m+1})$ of $\{1, \dots, m + 1\}$, the last card $\pi_{m+1}$ is **guaranteed to be one of the $m - n + 1$ normal cards**!
2. Furthermore, since all $m - n + 1$ normal cards have the exact same step value $a_i = -1$, conditioning on *which* of the $m - n + 1$ normal cards sits at position $m + 1$ gives the exact same count of valid prefixes $(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_m)$! Specifically, the valid permutations $(p_1, \dots, p_m)$ of the original $m$ cards are in exact $1$-to-$1$ correspondence with the $1$-valid permutations $(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_{m+1})$ that end with $\pi_{m+1} = m + 1$.

#### 3. Exact Double Count via Cyclic Shifts

Partition all $(m + 1)!$ permutations of $\{1, 2, \dots, m + 1\}$ into $\frac{(m + 1)!}{m + 1} = m!$ cyclic-shift equivalence classes, each of size $m + 1$.

By **Theorem 11.2 (Raney's Cycle Lemma)** with $k = 1$, within each cyclic class of $m + 1$ shifts, **literally $1$ cyclic shift out of the $m + 1$ shifts is $1$-valid**! Therefore, the total number of $1$-valid permutations of $\{1, 2, \dots, m + 1\}$ is
$$
N_{\text{total}} = \frac{(m + 1)!}{m + 1} = m!.
$$
By symmetry among the $m - n + 1$ normal cards (all of which have identical step weight $-1$, and one of which must occupy position $\pi_{m+1}$), the fraction of $1$-valid permutations that specifically place the dummy card $\pi_{m+1} = m + 1$ at the end is $\frac{1}{m - n + 1}$.

Let us verify this on the small hand-checkable cases $m = 2$ and $m = 3$:

- For $n = 1, w_1 = 2 \implies m = 2$ ($1$ special card of weight $2$, and $m - n = 1$ normal card of weight $0$), the two permutations of $(w_1 = 2, w_2 = 0)$ are:
  - $(2, 0)$: hand size goes $1 \xrightarrow{+1} 2 \xrightarrow{-1} 1 \ge 1$ (**Valid**).
  - $(0, 2)$: hand size goes $1 \xrightarrow{-1} \mathbf{0}$ after the first card, leaving no cards in hand to play the second card (**Invalid**).
  Indeed, $\frac{m!}{m - n + 1} = \frac{2!}{2 - 1 + 1} = \mathbf{1}$.
- For $n = 1, w_1 = 3 \implies m = 3$ (one card of weight $3$, two distinct normal cards $0_A, 0_B$), the valid permutations must start with $3$, so $(3, 0_A, 0_B)$ and $(3, 0_B, 0_A)$ are valid ($2$ out of $6$), matching $\frac{m!}{m - n + 1} = \frac{3!}{3 - 1 + 1} = \mathbf{2}$.

Thus, dividing $N_{\text{total}} = m!$ by the $m - n + 1$ symmetric normal cards gives the exact answer for distinct cards:
$$
\text{Ans}_{\text{distinct}} = \frac{m!}{m - n + 1} \pmod{998244353},
$$
and when the $m - n$ normal cards are treated as indistinguishable (as in Luogu P6672, where you choose the sequence of card *types* and the $m - n$ zero-weight cards are identical, dividing by $(m - n)!$), we divide $\text{Ans}_{\text{distinct}}$ by $(m - n)!$ to obtain:
$$
\text{Ans}_{\text{Luogu P6672}} = \frac{m!}{(m - n + 1)!} = \prod_{j = m - n + 2}^{m} j \pmod{998244353}.
$$
In fact, this product of $n - 1$ integers runs in **$O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space**!

::: {.callout-important}
## Algorithm Contract (`#196` Luogu P6672 — Raney's Cycle Lemma on Card-Draw Permutations)

- **Input**: Number of special cards $n \le 40$ and positive integer weights $w_1, \dots, w_n$ with $m = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i \le 10^5$.
- **Output**: Number of valid card sequences modulo $998244353$.
- **Index & Truncation Boundaries**: If $n = 0$ (so $m = 0$), return $1$; otherwise multiply $j$ over the integer range $[m - n + 2, m]$ (an empty product equals $1$ when $n = 1$).
- **1-Sentence Loop Invariant**: After multiplying $j$ from $m - n + 2$ up to $r$, the accumulator holds the falling factorial $\frac{r!}{(m - n + 1)!} \bmod p$.
- **Complexity**: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
:::

### Intermediate 2 (`#201`) — [KrOI2021] 蕾切尔 / Krzyżówka (Catalan Kernel Substitution $x = \frac{u}{(1+u)^2}$)

- **Source**: [Luogu P7439 — [KrOI2021] 蕾切尔](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P7439) (Curriculum Pool `#201`, `3B#29`)
- **Prerequisites**: Chapter 2 (Polynomial Taylor shift & convolution), §11.1 (Theorem 11.1 Formal Change of Variables), §11.3.1 (Catalan series)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

You are given a degree-$n$ polynomial $C(t) = \sum_{i=0}^n c_i t^i \in \mathbb{F}_p[t]$ ($n \le 10^5$, $p = 998244353$) and a target coefficient index $K \ge n$ ($K \le 10^7$). Define the formal power series
$$
A(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4x}} \sum_{i=0}^n c_i x^i (1 - 4x)^{-i} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4x}} C\!\left(\frac{x}{1 - 4x}\right).
$$
Compute $[x^K] A(x) \bmod 998244353$ (and show in the solution how the same Catalan residue substitution also evaluates the unweighted series $[x^K] C\!\left(\frac{x}{1 - 4x}\right)$ and transforms the polynomial coefficients in $O(n \log n)$ time).

**Required Complexity**: $O(n \log n + K)$ time and $O(n)$ space.

**Sample Trace ($N \le 4$):** Take $n = 1$, $C(t) = 1 + t$ ($c_0 = 1, c_1 = 1$), and $K = 2$. Then $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4x}} = \sum_{m \ge 0} \binom{2m}{m} x^m = 1 + 2x + 6x^2 + \dots$ and $\frac{x}{(1-4x)^{3/2}} = \sum_{m \ge 1} m \binom{2m}{m} x^m = x + 4x^2 + \dots$, so $[x^2] A(x) = 6 + 4 = 10$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model</summary>

Look at the algebraic factor $1 - 4x$ (and $\sqrt{1 - 4x}$). Why does $1 - 4x$ appear everywhere in Catalan generating functions, and what rational substitution $x = G(u) \in \mathcal{G}_1(\mathbb{F}_p)$ collapses $1 - 4x$ into a **perfect square** of a rational function in $u$?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad</summary>

Use the **Catalan change of variables** $x = G(u) = \frac{u}{(1 + u)^2} \in \mathcal{G}_1(\mathbb{F}_p)$:

1. $1 - 4x = 1 - \frac{4u}{(1 + u)^2} = \frac{(1 + u)^2 - 4u}{(1 + u)^2} = \left(\frac{1 - u}{1 + u}\right)^2$.
2. Therefore $\sqrt{1 - 4x} = \frac{1 - u}{1 + u}$, and the rational argument $\frac{x}{1 - 4x}$ becomes $\frac{u / (1 + u)^2}{(1 - u)^2 / (1 + u)^2} = \frac{u}{(1 - u)^2}$!
3. Also compute $G'(u) = \frac{d}{du}\left(\frac{u}{(1+u)^2}\right) = \frac{1 - u}{(1 + u)^3}$.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract</summary>

Apply Theorem 11.1 to $[x^K] A(x) = \operatorname{Res}_{x=0} A(x) x^{-K-1}\,dx$ with $x = \frac{u}{(1+u)^2}$, or expand $C\!\left(\frac{u}{(1-u)^2}\right)$ in powers of $\frac{1}{1-u}$ via a polynomial Taylor shift $v = 1 - u$ in $O(n \log n)$ time!

</details>

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation & Solution"}

#### 1. The Universal Catalan Substitution $x = \frac{u}{(1 + u)^2}$

Whenever a generating function involves powers of $(1 - 4x)$, $\sqrt{1 - 4x}$, or the Catalan series $C_{\text{Cat}}(x) = \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - 4x}}{2x}$, the canonical formal residue change of variables is
$$
x = G(u) := \frac{u}{(1 + u)^2} \in \mathcal{G}_1(\mathbb{F}_p).
$$
Let us record the exact dictionary of how every Catalan building block transforms under $x = \frac{u}{(1 + u)^2}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
1 - 4x &= 1 - \frac{4u}{(1 + u)^2} = \left(\frac{1 - u}{1 + u}\right)^2, &
\sqrt{1 - 4x} &= \frac{1 - u}{1 + u}, \\
C_{\text{Cat}}(x) &= 1 + u, &
\frac{x}{1 - 4x} &= \frac{u}{(1 - u)^2}, \\
G'(u) &= \frac{(1 + u)^2 - 2u(1 + u)}{(1 + u)^4} = \frac{1 - u}{(1 + u)^3}, &
\frac{G'(u)}{\sqrt{1 - 4x}} &= \frac{1}{(1 + u)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

#### 2. Applying Theorem 11.1 to Extract $[x^K] A(x)$

By Definition 11.2 and Theorem 11.1 (Jacobi's Formal Change-of-Variables Formula), for the unweighted series $C\!\left(\frac{x}{1 - 4x}\right)$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
[x^K] C\!\left(\frac{x}{1 - 4x}\right) &= \operatorname{Res}_{x=0} C\!\left(\frac{x}{1 - 4x}\right) \frac{dx}{x^{K+1}} \\
&= \operatorname{Res}_{u=0} C\!\left(\frac{u}{(1 - u)^2}\right) \frac{(1 + u)^{2K + 2}}{u^{K+1}} \cdot \frac{1 - u}{(1 + u)^3}\,du \\
&= [u^K] \left( C\!\left(\frac{u}{(1 - u)^2}\right) (1 - u) (1 + u)^{2K - 1} \right).
\end{aligned}
$$
Similarly, for the $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4x}}$-weighted series $A(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4x}} C\!\left(\frac{x}{1 - 4x}\right)$, the factor $\frac{1-u}{1+u}$ cancels cleanly with $G'(u)$:
$$
[x^K] \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 4x}} C\!\left(\frac{x}{1 - 4x}\right)\right) = [u^K] \left( C\!\left(\frac{u}{(1 - u)^2}\right) (1 + u)^{2K} \right).
$$

#### 3. Direct Extraction & $O(n \log n)$ Basis Conversion via Taylor Shift at $u = 1$

1. **Direct Coefficient Extraction in $x$**: For each $i \in \{0, \dots, n\}$, the $i$-th term of $C\!\left(\frac{x}{1-4x}\right)$ contributes
   $$
   [x^K] \Bigl( x^i (1 - 4x)^{-i} \Bigr) = [x^{K - i}] (1 - 4x)^{-i} = 4^{K - i} \binom{K - 1}{i - 1} \quad (i \ge 1),
   $$
   and for $A(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4x}} C\!\left(\frac{x}{1-4x}\right)$, $[x^{K-i}](1-4x)^{-i-1/2} = \binom{2K}{K} \frac{\binom{K}{i}}{\binom{2i}{i}}$, which sums in $O(n + K)$ time!
2. **$u$-Plane Taylor Shift for General Rational Multipliers**: When extra rational factors in $u$ are present in the $u$-plane residue $[u^K]\bigl(C(u/(1-u)^2)(1+u)^{2K}\bigr)$, we can also convert $C\!\left(\frac{u}{(1 - u)^2}\right) = (1 - u)^{-2n} \sum_{i=0}^n c_i u^i (1 - u)^{2(n - i)}$ into a partial-fraction sum $\sum_{j=0}^{2n} d_j (1 - u)^{-j}$ by substituting $v = 1 - u \iff u = 1 - v$:
   $$
   \sum_{i=0}^n c_i u^i (1 - u)^{2(n - i)} = \sum_{i=0}^n c_i (1 - v)^i v^{2n - 2i},
   $$
   which reduces to a single polynomial convolution / Taylor shift in **$O(n \log n)$ time**!

::: {.callout-important}
## Algorithm Contract (`#201` Luogu P7439 — KrOI2021 蕾切尔)

- **Input**: Degree-$n$ polynomial $C(t) = \sum_{i=0}^n c_i t^i \in \mathbb{F}_p[t]$ ($n \le 10^5$) and target index $K \ge n$ ($K \le 10^7$).
- **Output**: $[x^K] A(x) \bmod 998244353$.
- **Index & Truncation Boundaries**: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to $2K$ (or $2n$ if using the $u$-plane expansion) and evaluate the sum over $i \in [0, \min(n, K)]$.
- **1-Sentence Loop Invariant**: After processing $i \in [0, r]$, the accumulator stores $\sum_{j=0}^r c_j [x^{K-j}] (1 - 4x)^{-j - 1/2} \bmod p$.
- **Complexity**: $O(n \log n + K)$ time and $O(n)$ (or $O(K)$) space.
:::

### Advanced 1 (`#010`) — Ball (Bivariate Root-Shift & 2-Colored Bipartite LIF)

- **Source**: [AtCoder `fps_24_p` — Ball](https://atcoder.jp/contests/fps-24/tasks/fps_24_p) (Curriculum Pool `#010`, `1A#29`)
- **Prerequisites**: §11.1 (Theorem 11.1), §11.2 (LIF Form 2 & Form 6 Bipartite Good–Lagrange)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

Given two branching series $\phi_1(u_2), \phi_2(u_1) \in \mathbb{F}_p[[u]]$ with $\phi_1(0), \phi_2(0) \neq 0$ defining the coupled bipartite system
$$
u_1(x_1, x_2) = x_1 \phi_1\bigl(u_2(x_1, x_2)\bigr), \qquad u_2(x_1, x_2) = x_2 \phi_2\bigl(u_1(x_1, x_2)\bigr),
$$
and a factorized weight series $H(u_1, u_2) = h_1(u_1) h_2(u_2)$, extract the bivariate coefficient $[x_1^N x_2^M] H(u_1, u_2) \bmod 998244353$ for $N, M \le 2.5 \times 10^5$. *(In the solution below, we also show how the bivariate root-shift residue substitution solves the explicit ball-and-box rational generating function $[x^N y^M] \frac{(1 + x)^A}{(1 - \alpha x - y(1 + x)^k)^B}$ in $O(N + M)$ time.)*

**Required Complexity**: $O((N + M) \log(N + M))$ time and $O(N + M)$ space.

**Sample Trace ($N \le 4$):** Take $\phi_1(u_2) = 1 + u_2$, $\phi_2(u_1) = 1 + u_1$, $h_1(u_1) = u_1$, $h_2(u_2) = 1$, and $(N, M) = (2, 1)$. Substituting $u_2 = x_2(1 + u_1)$ into $u_1 = x_1(1 + u_2)$ gives $u_1 = x_1(1 + x_2 + x_2 u_1) = x_1(1 + x_2) + x_1 x_2 u_1$, so $[x_1^2 x_2^1] u_1 = [x_1^2 x_2^1] \bigl(x_1(1+x_2) + x_1^2 x_2(1+x_2) + \dots\bigr) = 1$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model</summary>

In the explicit rational variant $[x^N y^M] \frac{(1+x)^A}{(1 - \alpha x - y(1+x)^k)^B}$, extracting $[y^M]$ leaves $\binom{B + M - 1}{M} [x^N] \frac{(1+x)^{A + kM}}{(1 - \alpha x)^{B + M}}$, where the denominator root $1 - \alpha x$ can be shifted via a Möbius substitution. In the coupled system, $u_1$ depends on $u_2$ and $u_2$ depends on $u_1$: substitute $u_2 = x_2 \phi_2(u_1)$ into $u_1 = x_1 \phi_1(u_2)$ to reduce the system to a **single-variable implicit equation** in $x_1$!

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad</summary>

Treat $x_2$ as a constant parameter and view $u_1$ as a function of $x_1$:
$$
u_1 = x_1 \widetilde{\phi}(u_1), \quad \text{where } \widetilde{\phi}(u_1) := \phi_1\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr).
$$
Apply 1D Form 2 Derivative-Free LIF with respect to $x_1 \mapsto u_1$ first! What happens when you then extract $[x_2^M]$ from $\phi_1\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr)^N$?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract</summary>

When we extract $[x_2^M]$ from a function of $u_2 := x_2 \phi_2(u_1)$, since $x_2$ appears *exclusively* inside the product $x_2 \phi_2(u_1)$, for any series $A(w)$, $[x_2^M] A\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr) = \phi_2(u_1)^M \cdot [u_2^M] A(u_2)$! This completely separates the $u_1$-extraction from the $u_2$-extraction!

</details>

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation & Solution"}

#### 1. Formulation 1: Bivariate Root-Shift & Residue Decoupling

Consider extracting $[x^N y^M] \frac{(1 + x)^A}{\bigl(1 - \alpha x - y (1 + x)^k\bigr)^B}$ (or any bivariate rational/algebraic ball-and-box generating function where $y$ is coupled to a power of $(1 + x)$ and $(1 - \alpha x)$).

1. **Step 1 (Extract $[y^M]$ First to Isolate a Single Residue in $x$)**: Expand $(1 - \alpha x - y(1+x)^k)^{-B}$ in powers of $y$:
   $$
   [y^M] \frac{(1 + x)^A}{\bigl((1 - \alpha x) - y(1 + x)^k\bigr)^B} = \binom{B + M - 1}{M} \frac{(1 + x)^{A + kM}}{(1 - \alpha x)^{B + M}}.
   $$
2. **Step 2 (Root-Shift / Mobius Residue Change of Variables)**: To extract $[x^N] \frac{(1 + x)^P}{(1 - \alpha x)^Q}$ (or when $x$ is replaced by an implicit series $F(x)$), write it as $\operatorname{Res}_{x=0} \frac{(1 + x)^P}{(1 - \alpha x)^Q x^{N+1}}\,dx$. Setting $x = \frac{u}{1 + \alpha u} \iff u = \frac{x}{1 - \alpha x}$ gives $1 - \alpha x = \frac{1}{1 + \alpha u}$, $1 + x = \frac{1 + (\alpha + 1)u}{1 + \alpha u}$, and $dx = \frac{du}{(1 + \alpha u)^2}$, turning the extraction into
   $$
   [u^N] \Bigl( \bigl(1 + (\alpha + 1)u\bigr)^P (1 + \alpha u)^{N + Q - P - 1} \Bigr),
   $$
   which is a single polynomial product of two binomial expansions, computable in $O(N)$ time!

#### 2. Formulation 2: Complete Derivation of Bipartite 2-Colored LIF from 1D Form 2

Now consider the coupled bipartite system
$$
u_1 = x_1 \phi_1(u_2), \qquad u_2 = x_2 \phi_2(u_1),
$$
where we want $[x_1^N x_2^M] H(u_1, u_2)$ for $H(u_1, u_2) = h_1(u_1) h_2(u_2)$.

1. **Step 1 (Eliminate $u_2$ to Obtain a 1D Equation in $x_1$)**: Substitute $u_2 = x_2 \phi_2(u_1)$ into the first equation:
   $$
   u_1 = x_1 \widetilde{\phi}(u_1), \quad \text{where } \widetilde{\phi}(u_1) := \phi_1\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr).
   $$
   Notice that by the chain rule with respect to $u_1$ (holding $x_2$ fixed),
   $$
   \widetilde{\phi}'(u_1) = \frac{\partial}{\partial u_1} \phi_1\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr) = x_2 \phi_2'(u_1) \phi_1'\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr).
   $$
2. **Step 2 (Apply 1D Form 2 LIF with Respect to $x_1 \mapsto u_1$)**: By Form 2 (`另类拉格朗日反演`) applied to $u_1 = x_1 \widetilde{\phi}(u_1)$ with outer function $\widetilde{H}(u_1) := h_1(u_1) h_2\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr)$, we have for every $N \ge 0$:
   $$
   [x_1^N] H(u_1, u_2) = [u_1^N] \left( h_1(u_1) h_2\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr) \left(1 - \frac{u_1 x_2 \phi_2'(u_1) \phi_1'\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr)}{\phi_1\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr)}\right) \phi_1\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr)^N \right).
   $$
3. **Step 3 (Extract $[x_2^M]$ by Scaling $u_2 = x_2 \phi_2(u_1)$)**: Now extract $[x_2^M]$ from the expression above! Because $[u_1^N]$ and $[x_2^M]$ commute, let us look at how $x_2$ appears inside the bracket: **every single occurrence of $x_2$ is multiplied by $\phi_2(u_1)$**, i.e., $x_2$ appears *exclusively* through the combination $u_2 := x_2 \phi_2(u_1)$!
   Specifically, write the $x_2$-dependent factor as $A\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1), u_1\bigr)$ where
   $$
   A(u_2, u_1) := h_2(u_2) \phi_1(u_2)^N - \frac{u_1 \phi_2'(u_1)}{\phi_2(u_1)} \cdot u_2 h_2(u_2) \phi_1'(u_2) \phi_1(u_2)^{N-1}.
   $$
   For any formal power series $\Psi(u_2) = \sum_{m=0}^\infty \psi_m u_2^m$, substituting $u_2 = x_2 \phi_2(u_1)$ and extracting $[x_2^M]$ gives
   $$
   [x_2^M] \Psi\bigl(x_2 \phi_2(u_1)\bigr) = \psi_M \cdot \phi_2(u_1)^M = \bigl([u_2^M] \Psi(u_2)\bigr) \cdot \phi_2(u_1)^M.
   $$
   Applying this identity to $A(u_2, u_1)$ immediately decouples the variables $u_1$ and $u_2$:
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   [x_1^N x_2^M] \bigl(h_1(u_1) h_2(u_2)\bigr) &= [u_1^N u_2^M] \left( h_1(u_1) h_2(u_2) \left(1 - \frac{u_1 \phi_2'(u_1)}{\phi_2(u_1)} \cdot \frac{u_2 \phi_1'(u_2)}{\phi_1(u_2)}\right) \phi_1(u_2)^N \phi_2(u_1)^M \right) \\
   &= \Bigl([u_1^N] h_1(u_1) \phi_2(u_1)^M\Bigr) \Bigl([u_2^M] h_2(u_2) \phi_1(u_2)^N\Bigr) \\
   &\quad - \Bigl([u_1^{N-1}] h_1(u_1) \phi_2'(u_1) \phi_2(u_1)^{M-1}\Bigr) \Bigl([u_2^{M-1}] h_2(u_2) \phi_1'(u_2) \phi_1(u_2)^{N-1}\Bigr).
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   Look at the final result: it is the difference of two products of **completely independent 1D coefficient extractions**! Computing $\phi_2(u_1)^{M-1} \bmod u_1^{N+1}$ and $\phi_1(u_2)^{N-1} \bmod u_2^{M+1}$ via two 1D polynomial `pow` calls solves the entire 2D problem in **$O(N \log N + M \log M)$ time**!

::: {.callout-important}
## Algorithm Contract (`#010` AtCoder `fps_24_p` — Ball)

- **Input**: Series $\phi_1(u_2), h_2(u_2) \bmod u_2^{M+1}$, $\phi_2(u_1), h_1(u_1) \bmod u_1^{N+1}$ with $\phi_1(0), \phi_2(0) \neq 0$, and target degrees $N, M \le 2.5 \times 10^5$.
- **Output**: $[x_1^N x_2^M] \bigl(h_1(u_1) h_2(u_2)\bigr) \bmod 998244353$.
- **Index & Truncation Boundaries**: Truncate all $u_1$-series modulo $u_1^{N+1}$ and all $u_2$-series modulo $u_2^{M+1}$; if $N = 0$ or $M = 0$, the second product $[u_1^{N-1}][u_2^{M-1}]$ vanishes.
- **1-Sentence Loop Invariant**: Each 1D `pow` call maintains $P_1(u_1) \equiv \phi_2(u_1)^{M-1} \bmod u_1^{N+1}$ and $P_2(u_2) \equiv \phi_1(u_2)^{N-1} \bmod u_2^{M+1}$ so that the two decoupled dot products yield the exact $2 \times 2$ Jacobian determinant expansion.
- **Complexity**: $O(N \log N + M \log M)$ time and $O(N + M)$ space.
:::

### Advanced 2 (`#229`) — 小 Q 的序列 (Little Q's Sequence — Derivative-Free Form 4 LIF & Coupled Binomial Sum Linearization)

- **Source**: [LibreOJ 6703 — 小 Q 的序列](https://loj.ac/p/6703) (Curriculum Pool `#229`, `3B#27`)
- **Prerequisites**: Chapter 3 (`inv`, `ln`, `exp`, `pow`), §11.2.2 (Form 2 & Form 4 LIF), §11.2.4 (`Elegia`'s Coupled Binomial Sum Linearization)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

You are given a sequence of weights $f_0, f_1, \dots, f_n \in \mathbb{F}_p$ ($p = 998244353$, $n \le 2 \times 10^5$) and integer parameters $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \pmod p$. Compute the coupled binomial sum
$$
S_n = \sum_{k=0}^n f_k \binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k} \pmod{998244353},
$$
and show how the identical residue machinery extracts $[x^n] H(F(x))$ when $F(x)$ satisfies the bundled Form 4 equation $F(x) = G\bigl(x F(x)^\beta\bigr)$ with $G(w) = (1 + w)$.

**Required Complexity**: $O(n \log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space.

**Sample Trace ($N \le 4$):** Take $n = 2$, $f = (1, 2, 3)$, and $\alpha = 1, \beta = 1, \gamma = 0$. Then $S_2 = f_0 \binom{2}{2} + f_1 \binom{3}{1} + f_2 \binom{4}{0} = 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 1 = 10$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model</summary>

The summation index $k$ appears in three places simultaneously: in the weight $f_k$, in the lower index $n - k$, and multiplied by $\beta$ in the upper index $\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma$. Express $\binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k}$ as $[u^{n-k}](1+u)^{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}$ and shift the extraction index to $[u^n]$ so that all $k$-dependence collapses into the $k$-th power of a single series in $u$!

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad</summary>

This is the exact archetype of **`Elegia`'s Coupled Binomial Sum Linearization (§11.2.4)**! Rewrite $\binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k} = [u^{n-k}] (1 + u)^{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma} = [u^n] \bigl( (1 + u)^{\alpha n + \gamma} \cdot (u(1 + u)^\beta)^k \bigr)$. Summing over $k$ with $F(w) = \sum_{k=0}^n f_k w^k$ gives $S_n = [u^n] \bigl( (1 + u)^{\alpha n + \gamma} F(u(1 + u)^\beta) \bigr)$. Since $n$ is **fixed** here, we can either re-index $j = n - k$ or apply a formal residue change of variables $w = u(1 + u)^\beta$!

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract</summary>

Compare both $O(n \log n)$ routes for a fixed $n$:

- **Route 1 (Re-indexing $j = n - k$)**: Setting $j = n - k$ makes the binomial coefficient $\binom{(\alpha + \beta)n - \beta j + \gamma}{j} = [u^j] (1 + u)^{(\alpha + \beta)n + \gamma - \beta j} = [u^n] \bigl((1 + u)^{(\alpha + \beta)n + \gamma} \cdot (u(1 + u)^{-\beta})^{n - j}\bigr)$.
- **Route 2 (Direct expansion in $u$ via Form 4 / LIF)**: In $S_n = [u^n] \bigl((1 + u)^{\alpha n + \gamma} F(u(1 + u)^\beta)\bigr)$, substitute $w = G(u) = u(1 + u)^\beta$, where $u = g(w)$ satisfies the Fuss–Catalan equation $1 + g(w) = \mathcal{B}_{-\beta}(w)^{-1}$ (or $g(w) = w(1 + g(w))^{-\beta}$), whose coefficients have a closed form by Form 4 LIF!

</details>

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation & Solution"}

#### 1. Step 1: Converting the Coupled Binomial Sum into a Formal Residue

Let $F(w) := \sum_{k=0}^n f_k w^k \in \mathbb{F}_p[w]$. By the generalized binomial theorem, for each $0 \le k \le n$,
$$
\binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k} = [u^{n - k}] (1 + u)^{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma} = [u^n] \Bigl( (1 + u)^{\alpha n + \gamma} \cdot \bigl(u(1 + u)^\beta\bigr)^k \Bigr).
$$
Summing over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$ (and noting that terms $k > n$ would have $\operatorname{val}\bigl((u(1+u)^\beta)^k\bigr) = k > n$, contributing $0$ to $[u^n]$) yields
$$
S_n = [u^n] \Bigl( (1 + u)^{\alpha n + \gamma} F\!\bigl(u(1 + u)^\beta\bigr) \Bigr) = \operatorname{Res}_{u=0} \frac{(1 + u)^{\alpha n + \gamma} F\!\bigl(u(1 + u)^\beta\bigr)}{u^{n + 1}}\,du.
$$

#### 2. Step 2: Change of Variables $w = u(1 + u)^\beta$ via Theorem 11.1

To turn $F\bigl(u(1 + u)^\beta\bigr)$ into the simple polynomial $F(w)$, define the substitution $w = G(u) := u(1 + u)^\beta \in \mathcal{G}_1(\mathbb{F}_p)$, and let $u = g(w) = G^{\langle -1 \rangle}(w) \in \mathcal{G}_1(\mathbb{F}_p)$ be its compositional inverse. Let us express $g'(w)$ and $\frac{w}{g(w)}$ cleanly in terms of $g(w)$:

1. Since $w = g(w)\bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^\beta$, we have
   $$
   \frac{w}{g(w)} = \bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^\beta.
   $$
2. Differentiating $w = u(1 + u)^\beta$ with respect to $u$ gives
   $$
   \frac{dw}{du} = (1 + u)^\beta + \beta u(1 + u)^{\beta - 1} = (1 + u)^{\beta - 1} \bigl(1 + (\beta + 1)u\bigr),
   $$
   so by the inverse function theorem for formal power series,
   $$
   g'(w) = \frac{du}{dw} = \frac{1}{\bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^{\beta - 1} \bigl(1 + (\beta + 1)g(w)\bigr)}.
   $$
Now apply **Theorem 11.1** (in reverse, substituting $u = g(w)$ with $du = g'(w)\,dw$) to the residue for $S_n$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
S_n &= \operatorname{Res}_{w=0} \frac{\bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^{\alpha n + \gamma} F(w)}{g(w)^{n + 1}} g'(w)\,dw \\
&= \operatorname{Res}_{w=0} \frac{F(w)}{w^{n + 1}} \left(\frac{w}{g(w)}\right)^{n + 1} \bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^{\alpha n + \gamma} g'(w)\,dw \\
&= [w^n] \left( F(w) \cdot \bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^{\beta(n + 1)} \cdot \bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^{\alpha n + \gamma} \cdot \frac{1}{\bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^{\beta - 1} \bigl(1 + (\beta + 1)g(w)\bigr)} \right) \\
&= [w^n] \left( F(w) \cdot \frac{\bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^{(\alpha + \beta)n + \gamma + 1}}{1 + (\beta + 1)g(w)} \right).
\end{aligned}
$$

#### 3. Step 3: Computing $1 + g(w)$ in Closed Form via Form 4 LIF (Without Newton's Method!)

Do we even need Newton's method to find $g(w) \bmod w^{n+1}$? **No!** Look at the equation satisfied by $Y(w) := 1 + g(w)$:
$$
Y(w) = 1 + g(w) = 1 + w \bigl(1 + g(w)\bigr)^{-\beta} = 1 + w Y(w)^{-\beta}.
$$
This is literally the **Fuss–Catalan / Generalized Binomial Series (§11.3.1)** $Y(w) = \mathcal{B}_{-\beta}(w)$ with parameter $t = -\beta$!
Even better, look at the multiplier of $F(w)$ inside $[w^n]$:
$$
\Psi(w) := \frac{Y(w)^{(\alpha + \beta)n + \gamma + 1}}{1 + (\beta + 1)(Y(w) - 1)} = \frac{Y(w)^{(\alpha + \beta)n + \gamma}}{1 + \beta - \beta Y(w)^{-1}}.
$$
Compare the denominator $1 + \beta - \beta Y(w)^{-1}$ with the **Master Duality Table (§11.3.3)** for $Y(w) = \mathcal{B}_t(w)$ with $t = -\beta$:
$$
1 - t + t \mathcal{B}_t(w)^{-1} = 1 - (-\beta) + (-\beta) Y(w)^{-1} = 1 + \beta - \beta Y(w)^{-1}.
$$
It is **literally the Form 3 Jacobian factor of $\mathcal{B}_{-\beta}(w)$**! Therefore, by the Form 3 Fuss–Catalan identity $[w^m] \frac{\mathcal{B}_t(w)^r}{1 - t + t \mathcal{B}_t(w)^{-1}} = \binom{tm + r}{m}$ with $t = -\beta$ and $r = (\alpha + \beta)n + \gamma$, the $m$-th coefficient of $\Psi(w)$ has the instantaneous closed form
$$
[w^m] \Psi(w) = \binom{-\beta m + (\alpha + \beta)n + \gamma}{m} = \binom{\alpha n + \beta(n - m) + \gamma}{m},
$$
and even if we instead evaluate $[x^n] H(F(x))$ for a general bundled series $F(x) = G(x F(x)^\beta)$ where $G(w)$ is an arbitrary power series (not just $1 + w$), computing $g(w) \bmod w^{n+1}$ via one Newton/LIF step and one polynomial `pow` extracts $[w^n] F(w)\Psi(w)$ in **$O(n \log n)$ time**!

::: {.callout-important}
## Algorithm Contract (`#229` LibreOJ 6703 — Little Q's Sequence)

- **Input**: Sequence $f_0, \dots, f_n \in \mathbb{F}_p$ ($n \le 2 \times 10^5$), parameters $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \pmod p$ (and optional general series $G(w) \bmod w^{n+1}$ for $F(x) = G(x F(x)^\beta)$).
- **Output**: $S_n = \sum_{k=0}^n f_k \binom{\alpha n + \beta k + \gamma}{n - k} \bmod p$ (or $[x^n] H(F(x)) \bmod p$).
- **Index & Truncation Boundaries**: Truncate $F(w)$ and $\Psi(w)$ modulo $w^{n+1}$; extract the single anti-diagonal dot product $\sum_{k=0}^n f_k [w^{n-k}] \Psi(w)$.
- **1-Sentence Loop Invariant**: After processing $k \in [0, r]$, the accumulator holds $\sum_{i=0}^r f_i [w^{n-i}] \Psi(w) \bmod p$.
- **Complexity**: $O(n \log n)$ time for general bundled series $G(w)$ ($O(n)$ time for $G(w) = 1 + w$) and $O(n)$ space.
:::

### Mastery 1 (`#114`) — Slime and Sequences (Hard Version — Eulerian Bivariate EGF, Formal Residue & L'Hôpital Double-Pole Cancellation)

- **Source**: [Codeforces 1349F2 — Slime and Sequences (Hard Version)](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1349/F2) (Curriculum Pool `#114`, `1A#30` & `3B#15`)
- **Prerequisites**: Chapter 3 (`inv`, `ln`, `exp`, `pow`), Chapter 4 (Permutations & Eulerian numbers), §11.1 (Theorem 11.1), §11.2 (LIF & Laurent Geometric Series Trick)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

A sequence $a = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n)$ of positive integers is called **good** if for every integer $k > 1$ that appears at least once in $a$, the **first** occurrence of $k - 1$ in $a$ appears before the **last** occurrence of $k$ in $a$.

Given $n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$), for **every** $k = 1, 2, \dots, n$, compute the total number of occurrences of $k$ summed over all good sequences of length $n$, modulo $998244353$.

**Required Complexity**: $O(n \log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space.

**Sample Trace ($N \le 4$):** For $n = 1$, the only good sequence is $(1)$, giving $\text{Ans}_1 = 1$. For $n = 2$, the good sequences are $(1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1)$ (whereas $(2, 2)$ is invalid because $2$ appears without $1$), so $k = 1$ appears $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$ times ($\text{Ans}_1 = 4$) and $k = 2$ appears $0 + 1 + 1 = 2$ times ($\text{Ans}_2 = 2$).

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model</summary>

First find a bijection between **good sequences of length $n$** and **permutations $\pi \in S_n$**: given a good sequence $a$, list the indices where $a_i = 1$ in *decreasing* order, then the indices where $a_i = 2$ in *decreasing* order, and so on. Why is this mapping a bijection to $S_n$, and how do the ascents $\pi_j < \pi_{j+1}$ of $\pi$ determine the values of $a$?

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad</summary>

Under this bijection, the value at the $m$-th position of the permutation ($1 \le m \le n$) equals $k$ if and only if the prefix $(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_m)$ of length $m$ has **exactly $k - 1$ ascents**. Because the relative order of $(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_m)$ is uniformly distributed over $S_m$, the number of permutations in $S_n$ where the $m$-th element produces value $k$ is $\frac{n!}{m!} \left\langle \begin{matrix} m \\ k - 1 \end{matrix} \right\rangle$. Thus
$$
\text{Ans}_k = n! \sum_{m=1}^n \frac{1}{m!} \left\langle \begin{matrix} m \\ k - 1 \end{matrix} \right\rangle.
$$
Now recall the bivariate EGF of Eulerian numbers: $\sum_{m \ge 1} \sum_{j} \left\langle \begin{matrix} m \\ j \end{matrix} \right\rangle u^j \frac{x^m}{m!} = \frac{e^{(u-1)x} - 1}{u - e^{(u-1)x}}$. Substitute $w = (u - 1)x$!

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract</summary>

Setting $v = u - 1$ and $w = vx$ with $\Phi(w) := \frac{e^w - 1}{w}$ reduces the problem to computing $c_j := \sum_{m=j+1}^n [w^j] \Phi(w)^{m-j}$ for $0 \le j \le n - 1$, followed by a single polynomial Taylor shift $P(u - 1) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j(u - 1)^j$. Express $[w^j]\Phi(w)^{m-j}$ as the formal residue $\operatorname{Res}_{w=0} \frac{(e^w - 1)^{m-j}}{w^{m+1}}\,dw$, apply the change of variables $z = e^w - 1 \iff w = \ln(1 + z)$, and resolve the simple pole at $z = 0$ ($w = 0$) when summing the geometric series over $m$!

</details>

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation & Solution"}

#### Step 1: Bijection Between Good Sequences and Permutations $\pi \in S_n$

Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be a sequence of positive integers. Construct a permutation $\pi = (\pi_1, \dots, \pi_n) \in S_n$ by writing down the 1-based positions $\{i : a_i = 1\}$ in **decreasing** order, followed by $\{i : a_i = 2\}$ in **decreasing** order, and so on.

- Within each block of equal values $a_i = c$, the indices decrease ($\pi_r > \pi_{r+1}$, a descent).
- Between the end of block $c - 1$ (which is the **first** occurrence of $c - 1$ in $a$) and the start of block $c$ (which is the **last** occurrence of $c$ in $a$), the "good sequence" condition says that the first occurrence of $c - 1$ precedes the last occurrence of $c$, which means $\pi_r < \pi_{r+1}$ (an **ascent**) at every boundary between blocks!
- Conversely, given any permutation $\pi \in S_n$, we must start a new value $c \leftarrow c + 1$ at every ascent $\pi_r < \pi_{r+1}$ (and cannot split at a descent because elements within a block must decrease). Thus, the map $a \mapsto \pi$ is a **bijection** between good sequences of length $n$ and permutations $\pi \in S_n$, where the value $a_{\pi_m}$ assigned to the $m$-th element of $\pi$ equals $1 + (\text{number of ascents in the prefix } \pi_1, \dots, \pi_m)$!

For a fixed prefix length $m \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, there are $\binom{n}{m}$ ways to choose the set of values in $\{\pi_1, \dots, \pi_m\}$, $(n - m)!$ ways to arrange the suffix $(\pi_{m+1}, \dots, \pi_n)$, and $\left\langle \begin{matrix} m \\ k - 1 \end{matrix} \right\rangle$ ways to arrange $(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_m)$ with $k - 1$ ascents. Since $\binom{n}{m}(n - m)! = \frac{n!}{m!}$, summing over $m = 1, \dots, n$ yields:
$$
\text{Ans}_k = n! \sum_{m=1}^n \frac{1}{m!} \left\langle \begin{matrix} m \\ k - 1 \end{matrix} \right\rangle \quad (1 \le k \le n).
$$

#### Step 2: Bivariate Eulerian EGF and Reduction to Powers of $\Phi(w) = \frac{e^w - 1}{w}$

Recall the exponential generating function of the Eulerian polynomials $A_m(u) = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \left\langle \begin{matrix} m \\ j \end{matrix} \right\rangle u^j$:
$$
1 + \sum_{m=1}^\infty A_m(u) \frac{x^m}{m!} = \frac{u - 1}{u - e^{(u - 1)x}} = \frac{1}{1 - x \cdot \frac{e^{(u-1)x} - 1}{(u - 1)x}}.
$$
Set $v := u - 1$, and define the unit formal power series
$$
\Phi(w) := \frac{e^w - 1}{w} = 1 + \frac{w}{2!} + \frac{w^2}{3!} + \dots \in \mathbb{F}_p[[w]], \quad \Phi(0) = 1.
$$
Then the bivariate EGF in $(x, v)$ is simply
$$
\sum_{m=0}^\infty A_m(1 + v) \frac{x^m}{m!} = \frac{1}{1 - x \Phi(vx)} = \sum_{r=0}^\infty x^r \Phi(vx)^r.
$$
Extract $[x^m v^j]$ from both sides (for $m \ge 1$ and $0 \le j \le m - 1$): on the right-hand side, $x^r \Phi(vx)^r$ contributes to $x^m v^j$ only when $r + j = m \iff r = m - j$, giving
$$
[v^j] \frac{A_m(1 + v)}{m!} = [w^j] \Phi(w)^{m - j}.
$$
Therefore, if we define the polynomial $P(v) := \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j v^j = \sum_{m=1}^n \frac{A_m(1 + v)}{m!}$, then its coefficients $c_j$ are given by
$$
c_j = \sum_{m = j + 1}^n [w^j] \Phi(w)^{m - j} = \sum_{r = 1}^{n - j} [w^j] \Phi(w)^r \quad (0 \le j \le n - 1),
$$
and once we know $c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{n-1}$, expanding $P(u - 1) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j (u - 1)^j$ via a single **polynomial Taylor shift** gives $\frac{\text{Ans}_{k}}{n!} = [u^{k-1}] P(u - 1)$ in $O(n \log n)$ time.

#### Step 3: Formal Residue Change of Variables & Explicit L'Hôpital Double-Pole Cancellation

To evaluate $c_j = \sum_{m = j + 1}^n [w^j] \Phi(w)^{m - j}$ for all $j = 0, \dots, n - 1$ simultaneously, rewrite the $m$-th term as a formal residue by factoring $\Phi(w)^{m - j} = w^{-(m - j)} \bigl(w \Phi(w)\bigr)^{m - j}$:
$$
[w^j] \Phi(w)^{m - j} = \operatorname{Res}_{w=0} \frac{\Phi(w)^{m - j}}{w^{j + 1}}\,dw = \operatorname{Res}_{w=0} \frac{\bigl(w \Phi(w)\bigr)^{m - j}}{w^{m + 1}}\,dw.
$$
Notice that the base $z := w \Phi(w) = e^w - 1 \in \mathcal{G}_1(\mathbb{F}_p)$ has the closed-form compositional inverse $w = g(z) = \ln(1 + z)$ (requiring no Newton iteration to invert).

1. **Change of Variables $z = e^w - 1 \iff w = \ln(1 + z)$**:
   Applying **Theorem 11.1** with $w = \ln(1 + z)$ and $dw = \frac{dz}{1 + z}$ gives
   $$
   \operatorname{Res}_{w=0} \frac{(e^w - 1)^{m - j}}{w^{m + 1}}\,dw = \operatorname{Res}_{z=0} \frac{z^{m - j}}{\bigl(\ln(1 + z)\bigr)^{m + 1} (1 + z)}\,dz = [z^j] \left( \frac{1}{1 + z} \left(\frac{z}{\ln(1 + z)}\right)^{m + 1} \right).
   $$
   The extraction index $[z^j]$ is now completely decoupled from $m$, while $m$ appears only as the exponent $m + 1$ of the unit series $Q(z) := \frac{z}{\ln(1 + z)}$.

2. **Summing the Geometric Series over $m = j + 1, \dots, n$**:
   Summing $Q(z)^{m + 1}$ over $m = j + 1, \dots, n$ via the finite geometric series formula yields
   $$
   \sum_{m = j + 1}^n Q(z)^{m + 1} = \frac{Q(z)^{n + 2} - Q(z)^{j + 2}}{Q(z) - 1}.
   $$
   Therefore, for every $0 \le j \le n - 1$:
   $$
   c_j = [z^j] \left( \frac{Q(z)^{n + 2}}{(1 + z)\bigl(Q(z) - 1\bigr)} \right) - [z^j] \left( \frac{Q(z)^{j + 2}}{(1 + z)\bigl(Q(z) - 1\bigr)} \right), \quad \text{where } Q(z) = \frac{z}{\ln(1 + z)}.
   $$

3. **Resolving the Pole at $z = 0$ ($Q(0) = 1$) via L'Hôpital Cancellation & Inverse Substitution**:
   - **First Term $\text{Term}_1(j)$**: Since $\ln(1 + z) = z - \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{3} - \dots$, we have
     $$
     Q(z) = \frac{z}{\ln(1 + z)} = 1 + \frac{1}{2}z - \frac{1}{12}z^2 + \dots, \quad \text{so } Q(z) - 1 = \frac{1}{2}z - \frac{1}{12}z^2 + \dots \text{ has valuation } \operatorname{val}(Q - 1) = 1.
     $$
     Define the unit series $R(z) := \frac{Q(z) - 1}{z} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{12}z + \dots \in \mathbb{F}_p[[z]]^\times$. Dividing by $Q(z) - 1 = z R(z)$ shifts the coefficient extraction from $[z^j]$ to $[z^{j + 1}]$:
     $$
     \text{Term}_1(j) := [z^{j + 1}] \left( \frac{Q(z)^{n + 2}}{(1 + z) R(z)} \right),
     $$
     which computes $\text{Term}_1(j)$ for **all $j = 0, \dots, n - 1$ simultaneously** in one `pow` and `inv`.
   - **Second Term $\text{Term}_2(j)$**: Write $\text{Term}_2(j) = [z^j]\left(\frac{Q(z)^{j+2}}{(1+z)(Q(z)-1)}\right)$ as a formal residue in $z$ and use $\frac{Q(z)}{z} = \frac{1}{\ln(1 + z)}$ to transform back to $w = \ln(1 + z)$ ($z = e^w - 1$, $\frac{dz}{1 + z} = dw$, $Q(z) = \frac{e^w - 1}{w}$):
     $$
     \begin{aligned}
     \text{Term}_2(j) &= \operatorname{Res}_{z=0} \frac{Q(z)}{Q(z) - 1} \cdot \left(\frac{Q(z)}{z}\right)^{j + 1} \frac{dz}{1 + z} \\
     &= \operatorname{Res}_{w=0} \frac{\frac{e^w - 1}{w}}{\frac{e^w - 1}{w} - 1} \cdot \frac{dw}{w^{j + 1}} \\
     &= \operatorname{Res}_{w=0} \frac{e^w - 1}{e^w - 1 - w} \cdot \frac{dw}{w^{j + 1}} = [w^j] \left(\frac{e^w - 1}{e^w - 1 - w}\right).
     \end{aligned}
     $$
     Because $e^w - 1 - w = \frac{w^2}{2} + \frac{w^3}{6} + \dots$ has valuation $2$ while $e^w - 1 = w + \frac{w^2}{2} + \dots$ has valuation $1$, their ratio has a simple pole at $w = 0$. Factoring out $w$ and $w^2$ shifts the extraction to $[w^{j + 1}]$ of a unit series:
     $$
     \text{Term}_2(j) = [w^{j + 1}] \left( \frac{(e^w - 1)/w}{\bigl(e^w - 1 - w\bigr)/w^2} \right) \quad (0 \le j \le n - 1).
     $$
     *(Sanity check at $n = 1, j = 0$: $\frac{Q(z)^3}{(1+z)R(z)} = 2 + \frac{4}{3}z + O(z^2)$ gives $\text{Term}_1(0) = \frac{4}{3}$, and $\frac{(e^w-1)/w}{(e^w-1-w)/w^2} = 2 + \frac{1}{3}w + O(w^2)$ gives $\text{Term}_2(0) = \frac{1}{3}$, so $c_0 = \frac{4}{3} - \frac{1}{3} = 1$, matching $\text{Ans}_1 = 1! \cdot c_0 = 1$.)*
   - **Combined Formula**: Both $\text{Term}_1(j)$ and $\text{Term}_2(j)$ are single-coefficient lookups from two fixed power series of degree $n + 1$:
     $$
     c_j = [z^{j + 1}] \left( \frac{Q(z)^{n + 2}}{(1 + z) R(z)} \right) - [w^{j + 1}] \left( \frac{(e^w - 1)/w}{(e^w - 1 - w)/w^2} \right).
     $$

4. **Final Complexity Contract**:
   - Compute $Q(z) = \frac{z}{\ln(1 + z)} \bmod z^{n+2}$, $R(z) = \frac{Q(z) - 1}{z} \bmod z^{n+1}$, and $\frac{Q(z)^{n+2}}{(1+z)R(z)} \bmod z^{n+1}$ via polynomial `ln`, `inv`, and `pow` in $O(n \log n)$ time.
   - Compute $\frac{(e^w - 1)/w}{(e^w - 1 - w)/w^2} \bmod w^{n+1}$ via one polynomial `inv` in $O(n \log n)$ time.
   - Subtract to obtain $c_0, \dots, c_{n-1}$, perform one Taylor shift $P(u - 1) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c_j (u - 1)^j$ in $O(n \log n)$ time, and multiply by $n!$ to output $\text{Ans}_1, \dots, \text{Ans}_n$. Total time: **$O(n \log n)$**, space: **$O(n)$**.

::: {.callout-important}
## Algorithm Contract (`#114` Codeforces 1349F2 — Slime and Sequences)

- **Input**: Integer $n \le 10^5$, prime $p = 998244353$.
- **Output**: Array $\text{Ans}_1, \dots, \text{Ans}_n \bmod 998244353$.
- **Index & Truncation Boundaries**: Compute $\ln(1 + z) \bmod z^{n+3}$ so $Q(z) = \frac{z}{\ln(1+z)}$ has precision $z^{n+2}$ and $R(z) = \frac{Q(z)-1}{z}$ has precision $z^{n+1}$; compute $(e^w - 1)/w \bmod w^{n+1}$ and $(e^w - 1 - w)/w^2 \bmod w^{n+1}$. Extract $[z^{j+1}]$ and $[w^{j+1}]$ for $j \in [0, n - 1]$.
- **1-Sentence Loop Invariant**: For each $j \in [0, n - 1]$, $c_j = \text{Term}_1(j) - \text{Term}_2(j)$ equals $\sum_{m=j+1}^n [v^j] \frac{A_m(1+v)}{m!} \bmod p$, so the final Taylor shift $P(u - 1)$ recovers $\frac{\text{Ans}_{k}}{n!} = [u^{k-1}] P(u - 1)$.
- **Complexity**: $O(n \log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space.
:::

### Mastery 2 (`#203`) — 2021 CoE-II E: 数树 (Counting Trees — 4-Subtask Grand Synthesis Across Characteristic $0$ and Huge-$N$ Characteristic $p$)

- **Source**: [Luogu P7592 — 2021 CoE-II E: 数树](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P7592) (Curriculum Pool `#203`, `3B#22`)
- **Prerequisites**: Chapter 3 (`inv`, `ln`, `exp`, `pow`), Chapter 10 (Newton's method), §11.2 (LIF Form 1 & Form 2), §11.4 (Characteristic-$p$ LIF & Base-$p$ Frobenius Decimation)

#### Problem Statement & Exact Constraints

We consider a family of plane rooted tree counting problems controlled by a branching weight polynomial $\Phi(u) = \sum_{i=0}^d \phi_i u^i$ with $\phi_0 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$ (where an internal node with $i$ children has weight $\phi_i$) and a root weight polynomial $H(u) = \sum_{j=1}^{d_H} h_j u^j$, so that the generating function $F(x)$ of trees satisfies $F(x) = x \Phi(F(x))$ and the target answer for $N$ vertices is $[x^N] H(F(x)) \bmod p$.

Solve all **four progressive regimes (Subtasks 1–4)** of the problem:

- **Subtask 1 (Small $N$, Standard Prime)**: $N \le 5000$, $d \le 5000$, $p = 998244353$.
- **Subtask 2 (LargeSingle-$N$, Standard NTT Prime)**: $N \le 2 \times 10^5$, $d \le 2 \times 10^5$, $p = 998244353$, querying a single $N$.
- **Subtask 3 (All-$n$ Simultaneous Query, Standard NTT Prime)**: Output $[x^n] H(F(x)) \bmod 998244353$ for **all** $n = 1, 2, \dots, N$ up to $N \le 10^5$ when $\Phi(u)$ is a sparse low-degree polynomial ($d \le 5$).
- **Subtask 4 (Huge $N \le 10^{18}$ Modulo a Small Prime $p$ Where $p \mid N$ Is Possible!)**: $N \le 10^{18}$, $d, d_H \le 20$, and $p \le 10^4$ is a **small prime** (so $N \ge p$ and $p \mid N$ can occur!).

**Required Complexity**:

- Subtasks 1–2: $O(N \log N)$ time.
- Subtask 3: $O(N \log N)$ time.
- Subtask 4: $O(d p \log(dp) \log_p N)$ time and $O(dp)$ space.

**Sample Trace ($N \le 4$):** For $\Phi(u) = 1 + u + u^2$ (Motzkin plane trees where each vertex has $0, 1,$ or $2$ children) and $H(u) = u$, iterating $F(x) = x(1 + F(x) + F(x)^2)$ gives $[x^1]F(x) = 1$, $[x^2]F(x) = 1$, $[x^3]F(x) = 2$, and $[x^4]F(x) = 4$. Modulo $p = 3$ at $N = 3$ ($p \mid N$), Form 2 gives $[u^3]\bigl(u(1 - u^2)(1 + u + u^2)^2\bigr) = [u^2]\bigl((1 - u^2)(1 + 2u + 3u^2 + 2u^3 + u^4)\bigr) = 3 - 1 = 2 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$.

<details>
<summary>Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Combinatorial Model</summary>

Each subtask probes a different algorithmic regime of the implicit equation $F(x) = x \Phi(F(x))$:

- Subtasks 1 & 2 ask for a **single coefficient** $[x^N] H(F(x))$ when $N < p$.
- Subtask 3 asks for **all coefficients** $n = 1, \dots, N$ when $\Phi(u)$ has small degree $d \le 5$.
- Subtask 4 asks for a **single coefficient** at huge $N \le 10^{18}$ modulo a small prime $p \le 10^4$ where $p \mid N$ may hold!

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2 — Algebraic Setup & Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad</summary>

- For Subtasks 1 & 2, use Form 1 ($[x^N]H(F(x)) = \frac{1}{N}[u^{N-1}]H'(u)\Phi(u)^N$) or Form 2 ($[u^N]H(u)(\Phi(u) - u\Phi'(u))\Phi(u)^{N-1}$) via one polynomial `pow` in $O(N \log N)$ time.
- For Subtask 3, since $d \le 5$ is small and we need *all* $n \le N$, apply **Newton's method (Chapter 10)** to solve $G(F(x)) = F(x) - x\Phi(F(x)) = 0 \bmod x^{N+1}$, then substitute $F(x)$ into $H(u)$ in $O(d N \log N)$ time!
- For Subtask 4, classical Form 1 fails whenever $p \mid N$ (Failure Mode #5). Use **Form 2 Derivative-Free LIF** paired with **Base-$p$ Frobenius Digit Decimation (§11.4)**!

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3 — Coefficient Extraction & Complexity Contract</summary>

In Subtask 4, define $A_0(u) := H(u)\bigl(\Phi(u) - u\Phi'(u)\bigr) \bmod p$, which has degree $\le d_H + d$. Then $[x^N] H(F(x)) = [u^N] \bigl(A_0(u) \Phi(u)^{N-1}\bigr) \bmod p$. At each base-$p$ step, extract $(k_0, m_0) = (k \bmod p, m \bmod p)$, multiply $A(u)$ by $\Phi(u)^{m_0}$ via binary exponentiation in $\mathbb{F}_p[u]$, and decimate every $p$-th coefficient starting at $k_0$.

</details>

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation & Solution"}

#### 1. Subtasks 1 & 2 ($N \le 2 \times 10^5$, $p = 998244353$, Single-$N$ Extraction)

Since $1 \le N < p = 998244353$ and $\phi_0 = \Phi(0) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$, both Form 1 and Form 2 of Lagrange–Bürmann Inversion apply directly:
$$
[x^N] H(F(x)) = \frac{1}{N} [u^{N-1}] \Bigl( H'(u) \Phi(u)^N \Bigr) = [u^N] \Bigl( H(u)\bigl(\Phi(u) - u\Phi'(u)\bigr) \Phi(u)^{N-1} \Bigr).
$$
Using Form 1:

1. Truncate $\Phi(u)$ and $H'(u)$ modulo $u^N$.
2. Compute $\Phi(u)^N \bmod u^N$ via $\phi_0^N \exp\bigl(N \ln(\phi_0^{-1} \Phi(u))\bigr) \bmod u^N$ in $O(N \log N)$ time.
3. Compute the single dot product $[u^{N-1}] \bigl(H'(u) \Phi(u)^N\bigr)$ in $O(N)$ time and multiply by $N^{-1} \bmod p$.

#### 2. Subtask 3 (All $n = 1, \dots, N$ up to $N \le 10^5$, Small Degree $d \le 5$)

When we need $[x^n] H(F(x))$ for **all** $n = 1, \dots, N$, running LIF separately for each $n$ would take $O(N^2 \log N)$ time. Instead, because $d = \deg \Phi \le 5$ and $d_H = \deg H \le 5$ are small, we solve for the power series $F(x) \bmod x^{N+1}$ directly using **Newton's Method (Chapter 10)**:

1. Define $\mathcal{P}(F) := F(x) - x \Phi(F(x)) = 0$. Given $F_k(x) \equiv F(x) \bmod x^{2^k}$, the Newton iteration is
   $$
   F_{k+1}(x) \equiv F_k(x) - \frac{F_k(x) - x \Phi(F_k(x))}{1 - x \Phi'(F_k(x))} \pmod{x^{2^{k+1}}}.
   $$
   Since $\deg \Phi = d \le 5$, evaluating $\Phi(F_k(x))$ and $\Phi'(F_k(x))$ via Horner's rule takes $d$ polynomial multiplications, so finding $F(x) \bmod x^{N+1}$ takes $T(N) = T(N/2) + O(d N \log N) = O(d N \log N)$ time.
2. Finally, evaluate $H(F(x)) = \sum_{j=1}^{d_H} h_j F(x)^j \bmod x^{N+1}$ via Horner's rule in $O(d_H N \log N)$ time and read off all coefficients $[x^1], \dots, [x^N]$.

#### 3. Subtask 4 (Huge $N \le 10^{18}$, Small Prime $p \le 10^4$, Supporting $p \mid N$)

When $N \le 10^{18}$ and $p \le 10^4$:

- We **cannot** use Form 1 because $p \mid N$ is possible ($N \equiv 0 \pmod p$ has no inverse in $\mathbb{F}_p$; see **Failure Mode #5**).
- We **cannot** use $\ln / \exp$ or ODE recurrences for $\Phi(u)^{N-1}$ because $p \le N$ causes division by zero at every multiple of $p$.

Instead, we apply **Form 2 (`另类拉格朗日反演`)**, which holds over $\mathbb{F}_p$ for *every* $N \ge 1$ without dividing by $N$:
$$
[x^N] H(F(x)) = [u^N] \Bigl( A_0(u) \Phi(u)^{N - 1} \Bigr) \pmod p,
$$
where
$$
A_0(u) := H(u) \bigl(\Phi(u) - u \Phi'(u)\bigr) \in \mathbb{F}_p[u]
$$
is a polynomial of degree at most $d_H + d \le 40$.
Now we apply **Base-$p$ Frobenius Decimation (§11.4)** to extract $[u^k] \bigl(A(u) \Phi(u)^m\bigr) \bmod p$ starting from $A(u) = A_0(u)$, $k = N$, and $m = N - 1$:

1. While $k > 0$ or $m > 0$:
   - Let $k_0 = k \bmod p$ and $m_0 = m \bmod p$.
   - Since $0 \le m_0 < p$, compute $\Phi(u)^{m_0} \in \mathbb{F}_p[u]$ (of degree $\le d m_0 < dp$) by binary exponentiation of polynomials in $\mathbb{F}_p[u]$, and multiply by $A(u)$ to get $B(u) = A(u) \Phi(u)^{m_0}$.
   - By the Frobenius identity $\Phi(u)^p \equiv \Phi(u^p) \pmod p$, we have
     $$
     [u^k] \bigl(A(u) \Phi(u)^m\bigr) \equiv [u^{p \lfloor k/p \rfloor + k_0}] \Bigl( B(u) \cdot \Phi(u^p)^{\lfloor m/p \rfloor} \Bigr) = [v^{\lfloor k/p \rfloor}] \Bigl( A_{\text{next}}(v) \Phi(v)^{\lfloor m/p \rfloor} \Bigr) \pmod p,
     $$
     where $A_{\text{next}}(v) = \sum_{j \ge 0} \bigl([u^{p j + k_0}] B(u)\bigr) v^j$.
   - Replace $A \leftarrow A_{\text{next}}$, $k \leftarrow \lfloor k / p \rfloor$, and $m \leftarrow \lfloor m / p \rfloor$.
2. When the loop terminates at $k = m = 0$, output $[v^0] A(v) \bmod p$.

By **Proposition 11.2**, the degree of $A(v)$ never exceeds $\max(d_H + d, d) = d_H + d \le 40$ at the start of any iteration. Thus each iteration multiplies polynomials of degree at most $d p \le 2 \times 10^5$, running in **$O\bigl(d p \log(dp) \log_p N\bigr)$** time and **$O(dp)$** space!

::: {.callout-important}
## Algorithm Contract (`#203` Luogu P7592 — 2021 CoE-II E: Counting Trees)

- **Input**: Polynomials $\Phi(u)$ of degree $d$ with $\Phi(0) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$ and $H(u)$ of degree $d_H$, target $N$, and prime $p$.
- **Output**: $[x^N] H(F(x)) \bmod p$ (or all $[x^1], \dots, [x^N]$ in Subtask 3).
- **Index & Truncation Boundaries**: Subtasks 1–2 truncate $\Phi(u), H'(u)$ modulo $u^N$; Subtask 3 runs Newton iteration up to precision $x^{N+1}$; Subtask 4 initializes $A(u) = H(u)(\Phi(u) - u\Phi'(u))$ of degree $\le d_H + d$ with $k = N, m = N - 1$ and decimates modulo $p$ until $k = m = 0$.
- **1-Sentence Loop Invariant**: At the start of each base-$p$ decimation step in Subtask 4, $\deg A \le d_H + d$ and $[u^k]\bigl(A(u)\Phi(u)^m\bigr) \equiv [x^N] H(F(x)) \pmod p$.
- **Complexity**: $O(N \log N)$ time for Subtasks 1–3; $O\bigl(d p \log(dp) \log_p N\bigr)$ time and $O(dp)$ space for Subtask 4.
:::
